changes.before: Remove only : IScored from Counter, leaving its public ReadScore method. Will Read<Counter> still compile?
changes.after: Require a generic input type to provide a known action.

before: A generic constraint states what the type argument must support. where T : IScored requires T to implement the IScored interface.
Because of that constraint, Read<T> can safely call item.ReadScore(). Without a suitable constraint, an arbitrary T is not known to provide that method.

Read<Counter> accepts Counter because it implements the contract. Read<string> would fail to compile even if you hoped the string represented a score. Constraints do not add methods to the supplied type. A class with a same-named method but no declaration that it implements IScored does not satisfy this interface constraint.
Expected behavior from this example: 6. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer task: Implement a second IScored class and pass it to the same generic Read function. Use a .NET 10 console project with C# 14; reading completion does not verify this local work.
after: A constraint is a rule for a generic type argument. It tells C# what the chosen type must support.
where T : IScored requires T to implement IScored. That interface promises a ReadScore method that returns an int.
Because the constraint guarantees the method, Read can call item.ReadScore(). Without that rule, C# would not know that every allowed T has this method.
The program prints 6. Counter implements IScored, and its ReadScore method returns 6.
A class must actually declare that it implements IScored. Merely having a method named ReadScore does not satisfy this constraint. C# checks that rule before running the program.
